results.finding: In newly diagnosed focal epilepsy, levetiracetam did not meet non-inferiority to lamotrigine for time to 12-month remission, and lamotrigine was the most cost-effective option.
results.source: Marson A et al., Lancet 2021;397:1363-1374 | The SANAD II study of the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of levetiracetam, zonisamide, or lamotrigine for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy: an open-label, non-inferiority, multicentre, phase 4, randomised controlled trial

results.finding: For adults with focal-onset seizures, carbamazepine, levetiracetam, phenytoin and zonisamide have Level A evidence as initial monotherapy; lamotrigine and gabapentin reach Level A only in the elderly.
results.source: Glauser T et al., Epilepsia 2013;54:551-563 | Updated ILAE evidence review of antiepileptic drug efficacy and effectiveness as initial monotherapy for epileptic seizures and syndromes

results.finding: Hippocampal sclerosis is classified histologically by the pattern of neuronal loss; on MRI it appears as hippocampal atrophy with increased T2 signal and loss of internal structure.

output.summary: Lamotrigine performed best in SANAD II for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy (Marson 2021); the ILAE evidence review grades levetiracetam, carbamazepine, phenytoin and zonisamide Level A for adults with focal seizures (Glauser 2013); hippocampal sclerosis has an ILAE consensus classification (Blumcke 2013).

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy and, under the 2024 MHRA rules, is not started under 55 unless two specialists document that no alternative works.
Do not perform a lumbar puncture without first excluding raised intracranial pressure or shunt malfunction.
required_recommendations: Start levetiracetam or lamotrigine as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy, chosen for the absence of interactions with baclofen and omeprazole, with attention to mood and sedation given his baseline cognitive impairment.
If the shunt valve is programmable, check and reset its setting after the 3T MRI.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.
Advise on work safety in the warehouse (no heights, ladders or moving machinery until seizures are controlled).
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, no meningism and a two-month history of stereotyped focal seizures: no indication for CSF, and a lumbar puncture in a shunted patient needs shunt function confirmed first.
Automatisms, an olfactory aura and postictal confusion leave no syncope question; no cardiac history or murmur.
The events are clearly epileptic (aura, automatisms, focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure); Holter monitoring answers no question here.
FDG-PET adds nothing to a first diagnosis with concordant MRI and EEG; it belongs to presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of right temporal lobe origin with mesial temporal sclerosis, secondary to remote neonatal pneumococcal meningitis (dual pathology with prior perinatal CNS injury)

differential.diagnosis: Focal epilepsy from the right frontoparietal encephalomalacia (extratemporal onset)
differential.key_features: The old hemispheric injury could be epileptogenic, but the olfactory aura, oral automatisms, right anterior temporal discharges and right hippocampal sclerosis place the onset in the mesial temporal lobe.

differential.diagnosis: Shunt malfunction with raised intracranial pressure
differential.key_features: Weeks of headache in a shunted patient raised it; no papilledema, the reservoir refills, and CT and MRI show no hydrocephalus or transependymal edema.
Mother had generalized tonic-clonic seizures, but his convulsion followed a focal impaired awareness seizure with leftward version and the EEG focus is right temporal.
Stereotyped olfactory aura, oral and manual automatisms, a convulsion with incontinence and postictal Todd paresis are epileptic.
Automatisms, two minutes of convulsion and prolonged postictal confusion are not syncope.

key_clinical_evidence: Olfactory auras, behavioral arrest with lip-smacking and right-hand automatisms and 10-15 minutes of confusion are focal impaired awareness seizures of mesial temporal type; with the convulsion they meet the definition of epilepsy.
The convulsion began with forced leftward head and eye version and was followed by transient worsening of the baseline left arm weakness (Todd paresis): both point to the right hemisphere.

Epilepsy-protocol MRI shows right hippocampal sclerosis plus chronic right frontoparietal encephalomalacia from the neonatal meningitis (dual pathology), which also explains the lifelong left hemiparesis.
Routine EEG has equivocal right anterior temporal sharp transients and right temporal slowing; the sleep-deprived EEG shows definite right anterior temporal discharges.
CT excludes shunt failure as the cause of the headaches and the seizure: catheter in place, no hydrocephalus.

patient.history_present_illness: This 24-year-old right-handed male with a complex neurological history including neonatal pneumococcal meningitis, VP shunt placement, chronic left spastic hemiparesis, and prior cervical spinal surgery presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. His mother reports that over the past two months, the patient has experienced at least three episodes of behavioral arrest during which he appears to stare blankly, becomes unresponsive to verbal commands, and exhibits rhythmic lip-smacking and fumbling hand movements with his right hand lasting approximately 60 to 90 seconds each. After these episodes, he appears confused and disoriented for 10 to 15 minutes, often unable to recall the event. The family initially attributed these episodes to daydreaming or inattention related to his baseline cognitive profile. Yesterday evening, while watching television, the patient was observed to suddenly stop speaking mid-sentence, begin lip-smacking, and then turn his head and eyes forcefully to the left. This progressed over approximately 30 seconds to bilateral arm stiffening followed by generalized rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting approximately two minutes. He was incontinent of urine during the event. Post-ictally, he was confused and somnolent, and his left arm was weaker than his usual baseline, returning to baseline over about two hours. Emergency medical services were called and the patient was transported to the emergency department. He had no prior seizure history despite his complex neurological background. Over the preceding weeks, the patient has also complained of intermittent headaches, which his family attributed to stress at work, and a vague sensation of an unpleasant smell that no one else could perceive, occurring several times per week for approximately one month. He denies recent head trauma, fever, or illness. He has not started any new medications, and there have been no changes to his baclofen regimen. His mother notes that he has appeared more fatigued and irritable over the past several weeks, with subtle decline in his already limited reading ability.
